body_markdown:
Leaving a car bone stock is impossible for some of us. It’s not about being smarter than the engineers who designed a car or the workers who assembled it; instead, the goal is often to take a one-of-many car and make changes that tune it closer to exactly what we want as the end product. Sometimes we improve things; other times we change things just to change things.


That in and of itself is not a bad thing. Personalization shouldn’t be looked down on when done in a safe manner, but we can all agree there are a few automotive modifications that might be more popular than their function warrants. We are going to talk about the other end of the spectrum today and look at a handful of overlooked or minimized tweaks that can be done to most vintage cars.


## Tires


[Eric Weiner](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eric-weiner/)


They’re the only four parts of your car that actually touch the road, so small changes can make a world of difference here. The only problem is that tires, more often than not, are unsexy. Doing the research to pick tires can be confusing, and ensuring the end product will achieve the desired change can be daunting. Used tires can be annoying to sell, and being stuck with a rough ride or more road noise than desired until those tires age or wear out results in nothing but a constant reminder of a mistake.


Get tires right, though, and it can transform a car. OE-fit rubber is a game of compromise between brands that we, as the end user, are not forced to stick to.[Finding the right tire](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/classic-car-tires-everything-you-need-to-know/) for your usage can add a surprising level of enjoyment. This isn’t all about performance either. I put highway treads on my 2015 Chevy Express because its main purpose is highway miles. That modification made my long days looking through the windshield a lot easier, and my fuel mileage improved to boot.


## Driving School


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


For most of the people reading this, the most driving instruction you’ve received is a handful of lessons many years ago and maybe a 10-question test administered by a sleepy government employee. That’s a start, but it shouldn’t be the end.


Driver training is not always solely focused on extracting every bit of performance from a chassis. Oftentimes, it is more about better understanding what we are asking of the car while driving and how small changes on our end can make every drive safer. Track training might be warranted if you built or own a performance car, but be sure to understand the line between good track driving and good street driving.


## Suspension bushings


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


There are many parts of a car that are easily visible and therefore get a lot of attention when it comes to getting fiddled with by do-it-yourselfers. Suspension bushings are not one of those. Buried beneath the car and often held in place by crusty hardware, suspension bushings are underappreciated by most drivers.


Even if it is an involved DIY project,[replacing suspension bushings](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-to-diagnose-and-replace-bad-bushings/) with fresh OE units can totally revive the feel of an aging car, while “upgrading” to stiffer or more exotic bushing materials can further enhance or alter the ride. Regardless of what you install, be sure to follow the installation instructions and properly lubricate the parts. The squeaks and creaks that come from dried bushings can be maddening.


## Headlights


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


We’re not talking about a four-foot LED light bar in a truck grille here. Instead, think about taking the time to clean or polish the plastic lenses on aging lights or swapping out tired sealed beams for halogen or other updated bulbs. This isn’t only about seeing at night, either. Having headlights on during the day has been shown to reduce crashes, so having effective lights and having them on is a good idea. Just remember they don’t automatically go off on older cars. Coming back to a dead battery is never fun.


## Sound deadening


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


Most old cars are loud. Some are loud due to the exhaust. Some portion of that is even on purpose. While some seek out a borderline uncomfortable experience behind the wheel, that is not everyone’s cup of tea. Arriving at your destination with your hearing still intact can take a lot of work if you enjoy cars more than two decades old. Luckily, there is often a lot of low-hanging fruit if you want to make the cabin friendlier. Ensuring the doors and windows seal makes a huge difference and doesn’t require pulling the interior to add sound deadening—though you may want to do that too.


## Fresh touch points


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Similar to how the only four points that touch the road can change the impression of how a car drives, refreshing the steering wheel, shift knob, or seat can dramatically alter how one feels while driving. The experience of having a car that feels tailored to you is not something that has to be reserved for those special ordering from luxury brands. Even just fresh seat foam in a ’60s bucket seat can make driving a better time. New steering wheels and shift knobs are often easy to reverse if you end up not liking the change, and if a steering wheel puller is needed, they can often be rented for free from auto parts stores.


## Basic maintenance done on time


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Keeping your car from getting to the point where it needs radical transformation is often the best bet. Oftentimes it’s a worn part that spurs folks on to chase modification. Why[replace with OE-spec](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/5-tips-when-replacing-steering-components-on-your-project-car/) when it’s possible to upgrade? Well, that’s a slippery slope. More often than not, what we really want is the car to drive like it did when it was new, but too much time has passed for us to remember what that was. If fancy aftermarket parts exist, surely I need them, right? Self-restraint is a virtue, and for most of us, just keeping a car in well-tuned condition is more of an upgrade than we would care to admit.
